ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all proposed directors, shareholders, UBOs and material counterparties against the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, Canada's listed terrorist entities under s. 83.05 of the Criminal Code, and federal sanctions regulations made under the Special Economic Measures Act; politically exposed persons (PEP) screening must follow FINTRAC guidance, with enhanced due diligence required for PEPs and persons from high-risk jurisdictions; results must be documented and retained for AML/CFT audit purposes.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (BC Registries and Online Services)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The legal name must be in English or French and must include a legal element such as 'Inc.', 'Corp.', 'Ltd.' or the French equivalents; names in other languages are permitted only as approved 'translated names' supported by a certified translation, and the transliterated Latin-script version must be submitted to the BC Registrar of Companies for prior approval.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If a name request is rejected, the applicant may resubmit a new name request online; for administrative reconsideration, a written submission must be filed with the BC Registrar of Companies within 30 days of rejection, attaching the rejection notice, supporting rationale and any required ministerial or professional body consents for restricted words; if reconsideration is unsuccessful, the applicant may reserve an alternative name or seek judicial review in the Supreme Court of British Columbia, as there is no separate statutory appeal tribunal for name clearance decisions.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted subject to conditions: the registered and records office must be a physical street address in British Columbia at all times, must be capable of accepting service of process, and must not be a post office box; a virtual office provider is acceptable if it maintains a physical BC location and provides registered office services, but a purely online virtual office without physical premises does not satisfy the Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c 57.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low; estimated annual probability below 5% for a low-risk EdTech subscription business with no statutory license; no routine unannounced inspections are mandated under the BC Business Corporations Act, although FINTRAC may perform compliance examinations of AML/CFT record-keeping and identity verification obligations.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (British Columbia), SBC 2002, c. 57 — ss. 17–20 (incorporation and certificate), ss. 114–117 (articles), s. 124 (directors), ss. 126–132 (registered records office), s. 232 (corporate names)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: BC Registry Services — Corporate Online, Ministry of Finance, Province of British Columbia
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Incorporation Application (Form 1) and Notice of Articles (Form 2) filed electronically via Corporate Online; Certificate of Incorporation issued under s. 19 of the BCBCA. Statutory filing fee: CAD 300 (approx. USD 220).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital (s. 52 BCBCA); incorporation is permitted with zero capital and no escrow or trust account rule applies. The authorized share capital is fixed in the Articles, and the directors may allot shares for such consideration as the board determines. Non-resident ownership is unrestricted at the provincial level, with only the federal Investment Canada Act, RSC 1985, c. 28 (1st Supp.) net-benefit review applicable above the specified transaction threshold.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: 1. That the shares of the Corporation be subscribed for and allotted to the subscribers as set forth in the subscription schedule appended to these minutes, and that the directors be authorized to issue share certificates. 2. That the registered records office of the Corporation be established at [address] in British Columbia, and the records office officer be appointed. 3. That the officers of the Corporation be appointed as follows: Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Corporate Secretary. 4. That the corporate seal, bank accounts, and accounting year-end of December 31 be adopted. 5. That all incorporation filings and ancillary registrations with the Canada Revenue Agency be ratified and confirmed. 6. That this resolution is effective immediately.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Name Approval or Numbered Company Election
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services — Corporate Online Name Request module (bcregistries.gov.bc.ca)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a name request through Corporate Online providing three prioritized name choices with the required legal element ('Ltd.', 'Inc.', or 'Corp.') per s. 232 BCBCA. Attach a Name Search Report and pay the CAD 30 name request fee. If no name is accepted, proceed with a numbered company (e.g., B.C. 1234567 Ltd.), which requires no name approval.
required_dossiers: Name Search Report from BC Registry
Consent of the name grantee (if applicable, s. 231 BCBCA)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name request is refused for conflict or public deception, the registry will note the rejection; remedy by resubmitting a revised name request (additional CAD 30 fee) or by switching to a numbered company designation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate counsel (in coordination with BC Registry Services)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Engage corporate counsel to prepare Form 1 (Incorporation Application), Form 2 (Notice of Articles), Form 3 (Articles), and Form 7 (Consent to Act as First Directors). Verify that the Notice of Articles designates a registered records office located in British Columbia, authorizes Class A common shares, and appoints first directors who meet the residency and capacity requirements of s. 124 BCBCA.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as First Director (Form 7)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a drafting deficiency is identified (e.g., invalid share class condition or missing director consent), remedy by amending the draft forms prior to filing; corrected forms may be resubmitted without registry penalty if no filing has been accepted.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Filing and Issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services — Corporate Online electronic filing portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File the executed Form 1, Form 2, and Form 3 electronically through Corporate Online. Pay the CAD 300 statutory incorporation fee by credit card or a BC OnLine account. Upon validation under s. 18 BCBCA, the Registry issues the Certificate of Incorporation (s. 19) electronically, typically within 1–2 hours; the certificate is conclusive evidence of incorporation under s. 20 BCBCA.
required_dossiers: Completed Form 7 (Consent to Act as First Director)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the electronic application is rejected at validation, the portal issues a correction notice; remedy by correcting the flagged data and resubmitting. The CAD 300 fee is assessed only upon successful issuance, so no filing-fee loss is incurred.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Canada Revenue Agency Business Number and Tax Account Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — Business Registration Online (BRO)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon receipt of the Certificate of Incorporation, register with CRA through Business Registration Online to obtain a nine-digit Business Number (BN). Open the GST/HST account (compulsory under s. 240, Excise Tax Act, RSC 1985, c. E-15, when taxable supplies exceed the current CAD 30,000 small-supplier threshold), the payroll deductions program account (RC-1) if employees are hired, the corporate income tax account, and the BC provincial program account.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA defers issuance of the BN pending identity verification, remedy by completing telephone verification through the CRA Business Window (1-800-959-5525) or by mailing certified copies of the Certificate of Incorporation and Notice of Articles to the local Tax Services Office.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Governance, Annual Report, and Municipal Business Licence
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services (annual report) and the local municipal business licensing office (e.g., City of Vancouver)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the inaugural board meeting to adopt the Pro-Forma First Board Resolution, issue share certificates, open a corporate bank account, authorize the EdTech platform subscription agreements, and confirm the December 31 fiscal year-end. File the first annual report with BC Registry within 15 months of incorporation (s. 50 BCBCA; CAD 37.50 annual report fee). Obtain a municipal business licence if a physical office or development center is opened in a municipality.
required_dossiers: Share subscription schedule and share certificates
BC Annual Report filing through Corporate Online
Municipal Business Licence application (if physical premises)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the annual report filing is rejected for arrears or address discrepancies, remedy by paying outstanding fees and filing an amended Notice of Articles online. If the municipal licence is refused on zoning grounds, cure by obtaining a zoning compliance letter from the municipal planning department or by selecting a permitted commercial-zone address.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable for ISIC 6201 (interactive language education software); no statutory industrial license is prescribed at the federal or provincial level. General sector oversight: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) for digital-economy policy; provincial: BC Ministry of Jobs, Economic Development and Innovation.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No operating or manufacturing permit is required. The only ancillary authorizations are (i) a municipal business licence (e.g., City of Vancouver Business Licence) where a physical office is established, and (ii) the CRA Business Number registration described in the formation SOP.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environment and Climate Change Canada (federal) and BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy — Environmental Assessment Office
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — 'Not Reviewable' under the Environmental Assessment Act, SBC 2002, c. 43, s. 6 and the Reviewable Projects Regulation; software-only EdTech operations involve no prescribed physical works requiring a full EIA or environmental registration.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable to cloud-delivered EdTech: no point-source wastewater, VOC, or combustion emissions. General compliance obligations: Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 (SC 1999, c. 33) for responsible e-waste handling, and the BC Recycling Regulation (B.C. Reg. 449/2004) for diversion of retired computer hardware; office energy consumption must meet the BC Building Code Step Code levels as applicable.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: WorkSafeBC occupational health and safety registration and clearance under the Workers Compensation Act, RSBC 2019, c. 26; municipal fire-safety inspection and BC Building Code life-safety compliance for leased office premises; no industrial civil-defense or explosives permit applies to a software office tenancy.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — federal tax administration; official digital portal: CRA My Business Account via Canada.ca; British Columbia Ministry of Finance through BC Registry / BC OneStop for provincial PST and Employer Health Tax registration.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign-incorporated entity must first obtain a federal Business Number (BN), which is the Canadian TIN for corporations, by submitting Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number) or by registering online through CRA My Business Account. If the foreign corporation begins making taxable supplies in Canada, a registered GST/HST account is part of the same BN application. The BN is composed of a 9-digit account identifier plus a program account suffix (for example, RT for GST/HST, RC for corporate income tax). For foreign entities without Canadian incorporation, CRA may issue a non-resident BN for GST/HST where the entity has no permanent establishment in Canada but is required to collect GST/HST under the Excise Tax Act. Before carrying on business in British Columbia, an extraprovincial corporation must also file an extraprovincial registration under the BC Business Corporations Act and obtain BC PST registration through BC OneStop if selling taxable goods or services in BC. No minimum capital is required.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no check-the-box or entity classification election for corporations; a Business Corporation is a distinct taxpayer under the Income Tax Act. For eligible Canadian corporations, available elections include: (i) functional currency reporting election under ITA s. 261, (ii) non-calendar taxation-year election under ITA s. 249.1, and (iii) loss-utilization elections under ITA ss. 110 and 111. For British Columbia provincial tax, an election may be required for allocation of taxable income between provinces under the federal/provincial tax collection agreement; hybrid mismatch rules are automatic and do not provide an elective check-the-box mechanism.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) — federal value-added tax; British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST) — separate retail sales and use tax at provincial level.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: GST/HST: CAD 30,000 of worldwide taxable supplies in a single calendar quarter or in the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters, determined under section 148 of the Excise Tax Act (small-supplier threshold); once exceeded, GST/HST registration is mandatory. BC PST: remote sellers and marketplace facilitators must register if taxable sales to BC individuals exceed CAD 10,000 in the previous 12 months; no general threshold applies to BC-based sellers with an ordinary business presence.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not require real-time fiscal clearance, API clearance, digital stamping, or a government-designed e-invoicing network; CRA accepts electronic books and records if they are accurate and legible. GST/HST registrants must issue invoices or simplified receipts containing prescribed information (BN, date, description, tax rate and amount) for taxable supplies. Electronically filed GST/HST returns through CRA My Business Account are mandatory for certain registrants; PST invoices in BC must separately disclose the PST collected, but there is no pre-clearance or continuous transaction control regime.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: GST/HST zero-rating may be claimed for (i) goods exported in accordance with the Excise Tax Act as part of a sale and accompanied by proof of export, and (ii) services or intangible personal property (including EdTech subscription access and automated tutoring software) supplied to a non-resident person when the supply is not in respect of real property in Canada and not in respect of tangible personal property situated in Canada. For online language-learning subscriptions delivered through Apple App Store and Google Play, the place-of-supply rule generally treats the supply as made outside Canada if the consumer is outside Canada; the supplier must retain reasonable evidence of the non-resident status of the customer, delivery to a non-Canadian account or storefront, and payment settlement without a Canadian billing address. The supply is zero-rated for GST/HST purposes, and the registrant may claim input tax credits attributable to the zero-rated supply.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CBSA B13A or authorized reporting) for physical export shipments; not applicable to online-delivered EdTech subscriptions.
Bill of Lading / air waybill / courier export manifest for tangible goods; not applicable to zero-rated digital services.
Inward Remittance Certificate, bank wire confirmation, or payment processor settlement report evidencing receipt of export proceeds from the non-resident buyer.

For digital services and subscriptions: executed service agreement, non-resident customer self-declaration, IP address/geolocation logs, device/storefront country evidence, Apple App Store and Google Play sales/tax reports, and internal delivery logs showing no supply made to a Canadian recipient.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA and Canada Border Services Agency may reassess and reverse zero-rating, disallow input tax credits, deny refunds, and recover GST/HST with interest. Penalties for misstatements or fraudulent export claims include gross negligence penalties of up to 50% of the net tax sought to be evaded, minimum penalties for false returns, fines and imprisonment for tax evasion under sections 280 and 239 of the Excise Tax Act, and imposition of director/participant liability where a corporate claimant knowingly participated in a sham. BC PST authorities may likewise assess uncollected PST plus interest and penalties if the export exemption is not substantiated.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), prudential supervision by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), payment-system oversight by Payments Canada and the Bank of Canada; no dedicated foreign-exchange control administration exists in Canada
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains full current-account and capital-account convertibility under the Currency Act, Bank of Canada Act, and the repealed Exchange Control Act framework abolished in 1958. There are no balance-of-payment exchange controls, no prior-approval requirements for foreign investment, and no restrictions on profit repatriation. Dividends and branch remittances are freely payable abroad, subject only to Part XIII withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (base 25%, typically reduced to 5-15% under an applicable income tax treaty). The Canadian dollar (CAD) is a freely floating, fully convertible currency with an actively traded offshore market. For an EdTech subscription company incorporated in British Columbia, paid-up capital injections, license royalty payments, and intercompany service invoices are all remittable without exchange-control consent or surrender requirements. Practical hurdles are limited to banking AML/KYC due diligence and FINTRAC reporting obligations for Canadian-dollar and foreign-currency transactions at or above CAD 10,000.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no statutory timeline for the repatriation of export proceeds and no mandatory conversion ratio for export receipts. Exporters, including EdTech software and subscription-service providers, may hold foreign currency in USD or multi-currency accounts indefinitely without any surrender obligation to the Bank of Canada or Export Development Canada. Although no surrender rules apply, transactions of CAD 10,000 or more are subject to FINTRAC record-keeping and reporting duties under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act; financial institutions must also comply with Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) guidance on correspondent banking and sanctions screening. Corporates are, however, required to report certain cross-border movements of physical currency and monetary instruments in excess of CAD 10,000 via the Cross-Border Currency and Monetary Instruments Reporting (CBSA/Finance) regime.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium viability with mandatory Canadian registration. Canada functionally does not recognize the European/UK EMI licence or any equivalent 'Electronic Money Institution' passporting. Offshore digital EMIs such as Wise, Payoneer, and multi-currency platforms must either obtain an 'authorized payment service provider' registration under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA), administered by the Bank of Canada with transitional registration closing deadlines, or partner with a Schedule I chartered bank as the clearing sponsor. An offshore EMI cannot independently provide a Canadian bank account number or hold client CAD funds without RPAA compliance; the bank-facing treasury architecture should therefore treat EMIs as supplementary collection/settlement rails, not as the primary corporate banking account holder, to avoid OFSI and CDIC protection gaps. For British Columbia, a Canadian Schedule I bank account remains the fully viable custody and clearing base, with EMI rails used only for low-value consumer collections.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: At least one director or a designated officer with signing authority is ordinarily required to appear physically at a Canadian branch or with a corporate account manager in British Columbia for a first-hand identity verification (including original passports and valid visa/permanent-resident documentation). Several Tier-1 banks allow a fully remote onboarding video interview for low-risk domestic-controlled corporations; however, if any beneficial owner or director is non-resident, bank policy usually mandates either (i) physical attendance at the Vancouver or Toronto branch, or (ii) notarized identity attestation issued by a recognized notary or bank in the director's home jurisdiction, plus a video call with the corporate banking team. British Columbia corporations must also produce a Notice of Articles or a corporate registry search extract obtained on the same day, a certified share-register/minutes evidencing beneficial ownership, and proof of an operating address. The Canadian bank branch will additionally verify the business licence and source of funds for initial injected capital, and may require a reference letter from the parent or foreign bank where the ultimate beneficial owner exceeds 25%.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident directors and offshore beneficial owners owning more than 10% of the share capital
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (i) Certified passports and proof of residential address for each director/UBO; (ii) current BC corporate registry Notice of Articles and corporate search; (iii) notarized share register and ultimate-beneficial-ownership declaration; (iv) original bank reference letters from the home jurisdiction institution; (v) lawful-source-of-funds evidence including audited or signed financial statements and investment-commitment letters

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Digital-only EdTech business without a substantial physical office at onboarding (high account-opening scrutiny on operating substance)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (i) Signed commercial lease or managed-office agreement within British Columbia; (ii) BC or City of Vancouver business licence, as applicable; (iii) detailed 24-month business plan with revenue projections by subscription product; (iv) payroll or contractor records evidencing local substance; (v) active merchant platform reports from Apple App Store Connect and Google Play Console

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border subscription revenue and recurring FX flows arising from USD-denominated consumer payments via Apple IAP and Google Play Billing
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Apple App Store and Google Play Console monthly payout statements, payment processor settlement reports, treasury reconciliation schedules, underlying platform distribution agreements, and confirmation that end-user transactions are standardized low-value digital subscription fees under the applicable banking AML risk tier

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inbound capital injection from a foreign affiliated parent or strategic investor without operational history in Canada
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Notarized board resolutions approving the share subscription or intercompany loan, executed subscription/loan agreements with defined maturity and arm's-length interest rate, certified source-of-funds evidence from the remitting bank, parent company audited financial statements, personal net-worth or corporate financial capacity statements, and Canadian tax-residency clearances where relevant

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of potential counterparties or treasury vendor domiciles in jurisdictions considered high-risk or tax-haven under Canadian sanctions and FATF lists
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Underlying commercial contracts, invoices and purchase orders, beneficial-ownership declarations for each counterparty, sanctions/negative-media screening reports obtained from a reliable third-party provider, and management letters confirming no exposure to sanctioned entities under the Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital injections are executed via SWIFT MT103 or MT202 messages from the parent or overseas investor to the corporation's Schedule I Canadian bank account. Canada does not operate a foreign-exchange purpose-code approval regime; the remitter's narrative field generally states 'Share Capital Subscription', 'Paid-up Capital', or 'Intercompany Loan'. The Canadian receiving bank will require the corporation to complete a standard account-opening questionnaire and the bank to file an Electronic Funds Transfer Report with FINTRAC for any single inbound credit or same-day aggregate of CAD 10,000 or more (including outbound transactions). No Bank of Canada or OSFI prior notification is required for the capital injection itself, although banks must satisfy Customer Due Diligence on the investor and source of funds. Recommended routing: parent bank SWIFT payment in USD is accepted directly into its USD-transit account, with a same-day WesBank/CLS or correspondent FX conversion to CAD; alternatively, injection in CAD to avoid conversion friction. All in-bound investment documents, board resolutions, and subscription agreements must be archived in the corporate treasury folder for immediate production to the onboarding compliance team.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For trade settlements and vendor payables, Canadian corporates use SWIFT MT103 for single cross-border payments and MT202 for interbank cover. High-value CAD clearing leverages Lynx (the Canadian RTGS system, successor to the Large Value Transfer System); batch low-value retail payments run through the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS). For USD-denominated disbursements, the preferred structure is a USD correspondent account through the Canadian bank's US clearing bank, or a concentration account at a US correspondent, enabling cross-border payment in USD without double FX conversion. Where specific performance or repayment security is needed for content-licensing or infrastructure-provider agreements, an irrevocable Commercial Letter of Credit issued under UCP600 and advised/confirmed by a Schedule I Canadian bank, or a standby letter of credit (ISP98), is considered permissible. Conventional practice in the EdTech subscription vertical is to rely predominantly on SWIFT MT103 for licensing royalties and SaaS infrastructure payments, reserving documentary letters of credit for material distribution agreements with emerging-market counterparties where settlement risk or import-country regulatory approval is present.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Vanilla Over-the-Counter (OTC) FX Forward Contracts with a Schedule I Canadian chartered bank or approved counterparty
Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) for restricted-convertibility or frontier-market currencies where physical settlement is not feasible
Cross-Currency Interest Rate Swaps (CIRS) for long-term intercompany loan hedging (typically CAD/USD)
Plain Vanilla FX Options (European-style Call and Put structures) for revenue-protection and M&A-related treasury risk
FX Spot Contracts for near-term conversion of Apple/Google settlement proceeds
Currency Swap Transactions executed under an ISDA Master Agreement with a bank counterparty, including legally documented swap confirmation for material intercompany debt

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return (Form 4022) under the Canada Business Corporations Act, if the entity is a federal corporation registered extra-provincially in British Columbia
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due no later than 60 calendar days after each anniversary of incorporation or continuance; no grace period beyond the 60-day statutory filing window.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing can attract a prescribed late filing penalty; default for two consecutive annual return cycles places the corporation in risk of administrative dissolution by the Director after notice, followed by revival and reinstatement costs if dissolution occurs.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: British Columbia Annual Report for the extra-provincial registration (or company annual report for a BC domestic corporation)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, British Columbia Corporate Registry
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within two months after each anniversary of the date of registration or incorporation in British Columbia.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: A prescribed late filing penalty applies to annual reports filed after the due date; failure to file annual reports for two consecutive years can trigger administrative strike-off or cancellation after statutory notice, while revival requires a reinstatement filing and prescribed fees.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory audit threshold exists under BC or Canadian federal corporate law for a private, non-distributing EdTech corporation. A compelled independent audit arises only if the corporation becomes a reporting issuer under securities law, a shareholder or director demands and obtains an audit under the CBCA/BCBCA, the constating documents require one, or the corporation otherwise distributes shares to the public. There is no revenue or asset-size threshold.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: A private corporation in British Columbia may apply Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) under CPA Canada Handbook Part II; IFRS (Part I) is required for reporting issuers and is also available by election. Both are accepted for Canadian tax reporting when the accounting records are maintained in accordance with the Income Tax Act.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The CBCA/BCBCA significant-control transparency register is an internal register, not an annual filing to the BC Registrar or Corporations Canada. The company must update the Register of Individuals with Significant Control within 15 days after any share transfer or change in significant control. At each annual filing cycle, the directors must review and confirm the registered share capital, register of members, and transparency register for accuracy; share transfers require director approval and registration before the transferee is recognized as a shareholder.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (transparency register)
Minute Book containing resolutions and minutes of directors' and shareholders' meetings

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 300 – 1,200 per year for a British Columbia registered office and/or registered agent, depending on the service provider and scope of corporate secretarial support.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 8,000 – 25,000 per year for a voluntary or shareholder-required independent audit of a small private EdTech corporation; private non-reporting corporations normally incur no statutory audit fee.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction (federal 9% and BC 2% on first CAD 500,000 of active business income); Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) investment tax credit (refundable up to 35% for CCPCs); BC Digital Media Tax Credit (17.5% for eligible activities)

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T-2 Corporation Income Tax Return; filed electronically via CRA My Business Account or approved e-file software
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end

field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only Canadian-source business income; allocate based on permanent establishment
Claim only expenses directly related to Canadian-source income; maintain supporting documentation

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income (net of deductions and loss carryforwards)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply treaty provisions to determine taxable presence and income allocation

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal and provincial tax payable before credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Calculate using applicable rates; consider treaty withholding obligations

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax credits (SR&ED, investment tax credits, foreign tax credits)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only credits available under domestic law and treaty; attach schedules

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per full month (max 12 months); repeated failure: 10% plus 2% per month (max 20 months); daily interest on unpaid amounts at prescribed rate (currently 8% for corporations)

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim reduced treaty rate, non-resident shareholder must provide a Certificate of Residence (TRC) from their home tax authority. The payer must withhold at statutory rate initially, then the recipient may apply for a refund via Form NR7 (for dividends) or the payer may reduce withholding if TRC is provided in advance. For US residents, treaty rate is 15% (or 5% for substantial shareholding).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory: 25% for both royalties and interest. Treaty (US): interest 0% (subject to arm's length and non-resident ownership conditions); royalties 10% (for patents, trademarks, copyrights, and similar intangibles).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1 million for cross-border services; CAD 5 million for other controlled transactions
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not have specific Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) but applies the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) and requires economic substance for treaty benefits and foreign affiliate status. Transactions lacking commercial rationale may be recharacterized.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful omission of income, false deductions, or misrepresentation of cross-border transactions to reduce tax liability
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Penalty of 50% of tax evaded; criminal fines up to CAD 200,000 and imprisonment up to 2 years (Income Tax Act s. 239)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors jointly and severally liable for unpaid corporate taxes if they failed to withhold or remit (s. 227.1); travel bans and seizure of personal assets possible

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Incorporation without real business activity, used to artificially shift profits or avoid Canadian tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR recharacterization; denial of treaty benefits; penalties up to 50% of tax avoided; potential criminal charges for fraud
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be held personally liable for taxes and penalties if they knowingly participated in sham arrangements; civil restitution and potential imprisonment

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to implement AML compliance program, report suspicious transactions, or maintain records under Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 2 million for corporations; criminal penalties for non-compliance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally fined up to CAD 500,000 and imprisoned up to 5 years for willful non-compliance; travel bans and asset freezes possible
